newsitem.title: USA: Lawyers spar in Army rape case.
newsitem.headline: Lawyers spar in Army rape case.

text.p: Prosecution and defence lawyers battled over the credibility of alleged victims and the power of Army drill sergeants in closing arguments Thursday in the court-martial of an instructor charged with raping six trainees.
Prosecutor Capt. Theresa Gallagher described Staff Sgt. Delmar Simpson, the defendant, as an "mean, arrogant and manipulative" soldier who used fear and intimidation to rape women in his command.

Defence lawyer Frank Spinner told jurors there was reason to doubt the testimony of all six alleged rape victims and said the military risked a breakdown in discipline if jurors convicted Simpson without stronger evidence.
"If you convict Staff Sergeant Simpson on facts like these you're going to be sending out a message into the Army that no drill sergeant is safe," he said.

"What this really comes down to is any woman can come in and say she had sex with a drill sergeant, and she was raped, without any corroborating evidence," he said. "Discipline is going to break down, if it hasn't already broken down, because who has the power now? The drill sergeant or the trainee?"
The six-member military jury began deliberating shortly before 3 p.m. EDT. Four votes are needed for a conviction on any of the charges.

Simpson, 32, is the first of 12 trainers charged in a sexual misconduct scandal at the Army's Aberdeen Proving Ground to go to trial, although four cases have been resolved through administrative means or plea agreements. He faces 19 charges of rape and 35 other related counts.

His lawyers have argued any sexual relationships he had were consensual. But Gallagher, in an 80-minute closing statement, described in explicit, sometimes earthy, detail the prosecution's version of how Simpson allegedly raped each of the six women, some of them repeatedly.

"This is a case of rape. This is a case of the accused using his power, his easy access and his ability to control -- an unscrupulous drill sergeant grossly misusing his position to force his sexual attentions on trainees," she said. "He created an environment of fear, intimidation, and control."

Citing testimony of the women, she drew a picture of harshly forced sex in Simpson's office or elsewhere with limbs restrained by the accused, crying hushed by his commands and physical injury to the victims. She said Simpson became increasingly aggressive and forceful in his pursuit of sex with trainees during his time at Aberdeen.
"He becomes more perverted, more aggressive, more demanding over time as he becomes more experienced and more comfortable in his role as a drill sergeant," she said.

But Spinner methodicaly challenged the testimony of each woman, calling attention to inconsistencies and saying they all had motives to turn what was consensual sex into stories of force and pressure when told to the court or investigators.
"There is no physical, objective evidence that rape occurred," he said.

Simpson has pleaded innocent to rape and the other charges but earlier pleaded guilty to 11 counts of improper sexual intercourse with trainees and five of propositioning. He faces a maximum of life in prison if convicted of rape and a total of 32 years, dishonourable discharge and forfeiture of pay and allowances for the counts to which he has pleaded guilty.
